reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / ACR-EULAR classification criteria
clinicalPearls: Typically evolves through phases: a prodromal atopic phase of late-onset asthma and allergic rhinosinusitis, an eosinophilic tissue-infiltration phase, and a small-vessel vasculitic phase
Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia is a hallmark, and asthma is almost universal, distinguishing it from the other ANCA-associated vasculitides
ANCA (usually perinuclear anti-myeloperoxidase) is positive in only a minority, roughly one third to one half, so a negative ANCA never excludes the diagnosis
ANCA-positive patients more often have glomerulonephritis, mononeuritis multiplex, and purpura, while ANCA-negative patients tend to have cardiac and lung parenchymal eosinophilic disease
Cardiac involvement (eosinophilic myocarditis, cardiomyopathy) is a leading cause of death and warrants proactive screening
Mononeuritis multiplex causing asymmetric sensorimotor deficits is a classic and disabling manifestation
Remission induction relies on glucocorticoids, with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for organ-threatening disease, and anti-IL-5 biologics for relapsing or steroid-dependent eosinophilic disease
reference.pathophysiology: EGPA is a small-to-medium vessel necrotising vasculitis characterised by eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract alongside tissue and blood eosinophilia. It is considered one of the ANCA-associated vasculitides, though ANCA is detectable in only a subset. Dysregulated T-helper-2 immunity drives eosinophil recruitment and activation through interleukin-5 and related cytokines; eosinophil degranulation releases cytotoxic granule proteins that injure tissue, particularly heart, nerve, and lung. In ANCA-positive disease, autoantibody-mediated neutrophil activation contributes a more classic pauci-immune vasculitic and glomerular phenotype, whereas ANCA-negative disease is dominated by eosinophilic tissue infiltration.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count for eosinophilia and inflammatory markers
ANCA testing with anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase-3 specificities
Chest imaging for migratory or transient pulmonary infiltrates
Cardiac assessment with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, troponin, and cardiac MRI where indicated
Nerve conduction studies and tissue biopsy (nerve, skin, or lung) showing eosinophilic infiltration and vasculitis
Urinalysis and renal function to detect glomerulonephritis
redFlags: New heart failure, arrhythmia, or troponin rise suggesting eosinophilic myocarditis
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with haematuria and rising creatinine
Acute mononeuritis multiplex with foot or wrist drop
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage causing hypoxaemia and haemoptysis
Gut ischaemia from mesenteric vasculitis presenting as severe abdominal pain
reference.prognosis: With glucocorticoids and modern immunosuppression most patients achieve remission, but relapses are common and steroid dependence for residual asthma is frequent. Cardiac involvement remains the principal determinant of mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative ANCA excludes EGPA when eosinophilia and asthma are present
Overlooking silent cardiac involvement, which carries the worst prognosis
Attributing worsening respiratory symptoms solely to asthma and missing evolving vasculitis
Failing to consider that leukotriene-receptor antagonists or steroid tapering can unmask disease rather than cause it
references: ACR-EULAR classification criteria for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
